notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00525.opp-gr: In 1.1.1 a list of manuscript sigla from the edition's apparatus has intruded into the text after συνήλγησα τοσαύ-; it is omitted. In 1.3 'ἕκατ’ ἔρῳ' is read as ἑκατέρῳ ('each side'). In 2.2 'βούλους' is read as συμβούλους ('counsellors'). In 2.7 the main clause after the long parenthesis is resumed by 'ταῦτα τοίνυν ὁρῶσαι'.
13: 'πόλιν πόλιν μένην' is corrupt (a participle such as 'reproached' seems lost); rendered '[reproached]'. 27: 'περὶ τῆς φύσεως' taken as 'for their offspring'; the sense is uncertain.

§28: the text has a lacuna ('<εἰς> ...τητα'); the restoration 'temperance' (perhaps σωφροσύνην or σεμνότητα) is conjectural. §35: 'τόμενον' is corrupt, read as γινόμενον/πραττόμενον ('being done'). §39: 'invalid' renders the editorial supplement <ἀκύρως ἔχοντας>. §41: 'τίκα' read as αὐτίκα; the duplicated ἰδίους is treated as a dittography.

In 45.1 <δέ> is an editorial supplement, and ὰποψηφίζεσθε is read as ἀποψηφίζεσθε. That verb means 'vote to acquit' or 'vote against'. Here it presumably refers to acquitting the proposer of the decree, but the exact reference is uncertain. The last two lines (46.2–3) are not part of the speech. They are a Latin editorial heading from the printed edition, introducing the next group of declamations, and the second breaks off unfinished.

nodes.text: XXV.

In Corinth there was a handsome courtesan, Lais, who drew many lovers to her by her beauty. As a result, since many of the young were being corrupted, someone proposed a decree to expel Lais from the city. He carried it. After this, since many adulterers appeared in the city, and a law stood that an adulterer caught in the act should be put to death, many suffered the penalty under the law. And someone proposes a decree to bring Lais back again, while another man speaks against it. We declaim as the man speaking against it.
Preface.

1. I was pained in spirit and grieved to see such disgrace being prepared for Corinth, and some people trying to persuade [the city] to repent of what it has decided about Lais and wishing to undo what was well resolved. So I came forward to the platform, taking the part of a Corinthian, at least for the very time of the display.

Now the advocate of Lais has already enumerated adulteries and murders and the praises of the courtesan, showing up and down that it is advantageous to bring Lais back; we, however, go through what Lais did against us, and the vote already carried that she should not stay, and then that one must not change one's mind, nor should the city be disgraced among the Greeks by courting a courtesan, and things of that kind.

But if anyone, looking at the number of the things said, gives the advantage to our opponents, he has judged wrongly. For against all these things advantage alone weighs equal. Thus each side's case seems even, and the outcome is left to the time to come, whether one should ratify or annul the decree.
The Declamation.

1. I am ashamed, by Temperance, to see the city in need of advisers urging it to drive out licentiousness. For not to honour virtue straightaway and think it something to be longed for, but to give a hearing to those who pretend to plead for Lais but are trying to bring the city into disgrace, makes those who have lived temperately in any way at all hide their faces.

But since some have so disposed you that you tolerate them praising prostitutes, come, let us examine together what is advantageous, so that we do not go badly astray on the gravest matters by making those overcome by pleasures through love both our judges and our counsellors. For it is unreasonable that those who abet so outrageous a business do not hesitate to make their own shameful pleasure plain to the people, while we are seen to despise good order.

I, then, turn away from lawless unions, and I consider that those infatuated with them are not good men, so that it often occurs to me to reflect how certain people, wishing to outrage the laws, made it their practice to live such a life as brings the whole city into disgrace. For although it was open to them, if they did not wish to master their pleasures, to approach a girl's father and speak with him about marriage, and by showing a moderate character to achieve what they sought and satisfy their desire, a course in which they could both seem not to do wrong and the city could be well regarded among the Greeks, as being thought to have temperate men, they chose rather to despise the common advantage and to look on while their own life was dishonoured than to do anything that custom prescribes. A fine thing indeed to obey such a nature, which summons the city to outrage! One could recognise the excess of their shamelessness by hearing someone briefly narrate what happened lately.

4. Formerly we could pride ourselves on temperance no less than the other Greeks, for the city did not have Lais, and we all loved our own wives, so that it came about both that Corinth was well regarded by everyone and that its inhabitants lived in prosperity, the goodwill of the gods guarding the city. For the gods are by nature disposed to give those who practise virtue as rewards common prosperity and children proclaimed for their good birth.

This, then, was the good fortune the city enjoyed; but some malign spirit, begrudging the fortune it then had, brings Lais to the city from among the barbarians, for she was Sicilian, [a woman] clever at hunting youth and inciting it to outrageous pleasures, and able to render a wealthy city destitute; for a courtesan is a thing that lures youth. And, schooled in growing rich from such work, she emptied many houses of their money, now pretending to love a rich young man until she had kindled in him a longing that was not there, now fleeing her lover and inclining to another, inviting a larger gift of money, at other times provoking rival lovers to war and to compete with one another in gifts, by which victory belongs only to the one who outdoes the other. For prostitutes have this kind of skill in luring the young to spend their estates on them. For the man who loves outrageously thinks want bearable and would rather, I think, live with poverty than see his rival honoured by the woman he longs for.

From this she was able to harm the city in two ways. For all the wealth was carried to her, as the lovers vied with each other and tried by gifts of money to make her more their own, and the youth was no longer of any use to the city, neglecting military training and busying itself about Lais' doors.

Often she stirred respectable women to envy of her life, by being very rich and much sought after by the many. For when they saw their husbands neglecting their former affection for them, valuing the courtesan more and transferring the wealth at home to her (for it is customary for those who long for a courtesan to take away the very thing they see their wives most delighting in and give it to their mistresses, showing how far they prefer her to the woman given them by law), seeing this, then, they sometimes pretended not to know of their husbands' intimacy with Lais, and at other times, extolling temperance to them and making the strongest accusation of incontinence, they tried to bring them back to their former affection.

But when the husbands praised their words at home but were bewitched in the marketplace by the courtesan's speeches (for a prostitute is by nature able to persuade even a temperate man to despise virtue and to hunt him into love with intricate words), when, then, the evil was irresistible and in the end the husbands no longer even deigned to visit their wives, most of the women, honouring temperance, were able to keep to their proper bearing, but some, overcome by nature, judging Lais' life enviable and thinking they would thus take vengeance on their husbands, considered that they should sell their youthful beauty to whoever wished.

From this, I think, some men, avenging griefs and attacking their enemies' misfortunes, readily drew to what they wanted the women who, through being deserted by their husbands, thought Lais' business enviable. For a man who keeps company with a courtesan and joins his nights to his days is apt to provoke a woman to despise temperance. So the women, once they had tasted luxury, were no longer able to change their nature, but even now they still do wrong, unless some means should stop them.

10. As I am about to recount the disgrace among the Greeks of their sailing in to the courtesan, I hide my face, fearing for myself and the city, both because I bring to mind the misfortunes of my country and because I am compelled to say things unfitting for those who propose decrees worthy of Corinth; and I fear I may seem to be a hater of the city by bringing into the open what was not well done in it. For when something outrageous has been done, to be unwilling to keep quiet and blunt the injury by silence, but to wish to take vengeance for what happened, naturally tends rather to increase the outrage.

But since it seems a greater outrage to overlook a disease overwhelming in its magnitude and about to spread over Corinth again, and better to expose in speech what was done than to admit the beginning of a second wrong, I shall not hesitate to bring into the open what happened lately, even if the matter seems foreign to the character of the city and to my own conduct as a citizen.

12. All those of the Greeks into whom a passion for licentiousness entered, ashamed to make their wickedness plain to their own fellow citizens, since the notorious Lais was living as a citizen among us, as she ought not, and fearing correction at home, but having, it seems, recognised the licence among us, and perhaps also mocking the city because it is a base for licentiousness, sailed to our city, thinking it nothing other than a brothel-keeper.

For these reasons, then, by the providence, I think, of one of the gods, the decent and temperate among the citizens, seeing the city liable to every outrage, [reproached] and held fast by a blame hard to shake off, found one release from these difficulties: to transfer elsewhere the vice being practised. And they propose a decree concerning temperance, a fine one, by Athena, and foreign to the policy of those who speak for Lais: that Lais should no longer be in the city, but should go away and live wherever she likes outside the borders of the land, so that she might neither outrage our wives by mixing with them nor corrupt the minds of the young.

They ought, then, to have added that in future it should not be permitted to bring her back either, or else that death should be the penalty for anyone attempting to persuade [the city to do so]. For in that case Lais's fine advocates would not have used these fine words: 'Yes,' they say, 'but since she was driven out, the young men wrong the women given [to husbands] by law, and many Laises have arisen in the city instead of one. So we must bring her back and satisfy the pleasures of the young through her. For in this way they will check their outrageous impulse towards free women.'

15. Those who advise such arguments ought to live in another city along with Lais, one in which they conduct public life without temperance. For if it were not possible to pass one's life, or simply to live, without licentiousness, I would advise bringing back not only Lais but many courtesans, so that we might live without fear, each keeping the wife who shares his house; but since I know that temperance brings honour to those who practise it, and I see that sensible men have devoted themselves to it, for it sets cities upright and procures the greatest glory and wealth of money, stop setting wrongs side by side and advising [us] to choose one and flee the other, when you should consider in each case what will be beneficial, and seek a decent pretext by which the city might be shown free of the harm of both.

By the gods, which seems better to you: to master both, or to ratify one by vote and stop the other? Perhaps you would admit the former, blushing. For it is not the one who errs moderately, but the one who is overcome by none of the base things, who would reasonably be thought happy. Let Lais stay, then, as she is, and our good name has so far been half achieved. For the young men, revelling around her, will not despise military training, nor will they spend the wealth they ought to spend on behalf of the city on costly feasts and drunkenness and shameful pleasures; and the city will not seem to have changed, matters which you too admit, unwillingly, to be good.

For by saying that you do not want to recall Lais for her own sake, but so that we may make the women in the city temperate, you showed that Lais's living in Corinth is not something to be chosen for itself. For if you had judged it a good thing without comparing it with some other, worse thing, you would not have added the reason, excusing the wrong by its apparent advantage. But if you think that women already overcome by pleasures, which you have thought to remedy by Lais's return, can be temperate, there are surely other ways somewhere by which we shall persuade them to keep quiet and not be carried away to outrageous pleasures.

For we shall not grant them licence to do whatever they like, but first we shall train their inclination by law, so that, shrinking from the penalty of the law, they may be compelled to be temperate; then, advising what is good with reasonable words, we shall try to win back those who have been corrupted not by the exile of Lais but rather, as I at any rate would say, by emulation [of her].

But if they look to licentiousness and do not accept our words, I for my part judge it better to deem these women worthy of the same [treatment] as Lais than to give Lais an addition to the evil. For if they see her granted such honour as a return, they will remain in the same inclination, thinking that this brings them glory. So for both the common good name and safety it will not be beneficial for any of the decisions to be undone. For since, if she stays as she is, she gives the impression that we fixed no slight [penalty] for women who act unworthily of the city, while if she is recalled she prepares the rest [of us] to fear for the remaining matters too, it is plain that by returning she becomes a pretext not for temperance, as you yourself say, but for licentiousness.

20. But everyone, unless they are very simple-minded, knows the intention of the decree, and they blame the city for allowing such men to propose whatever they like. Stop, then, abetting what is admittedly shameful under a pretext of goodwill. The city will properly teach the young to be temperate, driving away wrongdoing by the best labours. For it will compel those of fighting age to go hunting, to shoot with the bow and to use arms, so that there is no room at all for pleasures. For passion naturally arises from soft living and luxury. When this is removed, then, and the practice of warfare brought in instead, cares about these things subside.

But this fine fellow here, overlooking everything, devotes himself to one thing only, persuading [you] to bring Lais back, and has spent all his zeal on this, bidding farewell to the advantage of the city; for he is infatuated, it seems, with the woman and thinks that she alone has a brilliant bodily beauty, and so, serving his passion, he asks for the woman he desires.

Come now, by the gods, if, after you have accepted these charming words full of amorous verbosity, someone, seeing the great outrageousness, condemns the man who persuaded [you] to bring back, to the corruption of the young, a courtesan whom you drove out so that they might be saved, and the man who persuaded [you] says to his accuser, 'Fellow, why do you accuse the proposer rather than those who were persuaded? For I advised it then thinking it beneficial, but no one was compelling the city, if it did not seem right, to ratify it against its judgement' — if he says this, will he not make the wrong light for himself and lay the whole blame on you? Then how is it not shameful to put up with men saying things from which the wrongdoers will have a refuge of defence, while the city will incur the outrage of their licentious deeds?

Besides this, I do not think it natural to consider the same [person] the cause both of licentiousness and of temperance, and to banish her so that she may not lead the young into outrageous passions, but to bring her back again so that she may become a pretext for good order; as if someone, while his ship was running before a fair wind and the winds were blowing astern, sweet and gentle, were to turn the rudder about and travel in the opposite direction, thinking to accomplish the other voyage with the same winds.

And how, on this basis, could consistency be preserved? For if the exile was lawful, it is not beneficial to recall her; but if Lais's presence is profitable, why did we wrong the woman for nothing? For if, when the decree against Lais was being proposed, someone wishing to show her that he valued nothing above his goodwill towards her had come forward and tried to persuade [you] to annul the decree, would you have accepted his words, or, thinking that he was talking nonsense, would you not have refused to listen to him deceiving the people?

For if you think Lais's advocate speaks reasonably, why did you condemn the woman for nothing? But if, recognising the aim of a man enslaved to passion, you took no account of his outrageous words, how is it reasonable now to accept those who suffer from the same disease as he? And it seems to me absurd that a well-governed city, one which together with the Lacedaemonians put down the tyrannies of Greece, should act as bodyguard to Lais and consider how it will serve the outrageous pleasures of the young.

26. 'But it is better,' he says, 'to be occupied with her, and not to bring the city to a shortage of men through men being violently killed because of adulteries.' And how is it not better to be counted among good men easily numbered than to have a multitude that is reproached? For if the wickedness of one woman produces common misfortunes, what is it likely to do when it is carried over to many? But since you are so solemn in listing for us murders and the desolation of the city, for which she gave occasion though not present, having implanted a licentious disposition in the souls of the young, I shall not hesitate to say that I, for my part, would gladly kill the lawbreakers with my own hand; but when will you show as many killed lawfully for adultery as that foul creature has seen slaughtered most lawlessly around her workshop? How many women, seeing their husbands living with Lais, have wept for their widowhood, not even having children to console them in their misfortune? For she prevented many from having children, from whom cities naturally gain safety and become superior in number to their enemies.

For forces flourish when a generation always able to labour is added, and soldiers, running risks for their offspring, choose to fall nobly rather than live as slaves with their children. Lais, when present, prevented the citizens from taking thought for these things. So without noticing it, by the very means by which you defend Lais, you accuse her, and show her to be the cause of the misfortunes that happened both when she was present and when she was not.

28. Stop, then, preferring licentiousness to virtue and thinking that the one is the occasion of the other. Let us not incur such disgrace as to need Lais to bring the city to its senses. For if you say that she trained Corinth in [temperance], how do the other Greek cities govern themselves without Lais? And how, if the common end overtakes her (would that she had never come into the light at all!), will the city live temperately?

You will say, I know well, that before she dies she will produce many Laises for the city. For this is in fact what you are eager for: to show that we alone, beyond all others, suffer from the disease of incontinence. Tell me, did the city have this bad name before Lais lived in Corinth, or did the disease come in along with her? No one so dishonours justice as to find any fault with our ancient ways. So, since nothing shameful happened before her, she is shown to be the cause of the later disgrace.

30. I want to tell you briefly what our state was before the courtesan burst into the city. We were the ones who displayed triremes on the sea, and we were admired for the novelty of the workmanship. Indeed, later, when the Samians were building ships, we sent them men skilled in this craft. Nor was it enough only to invent them; we also used them in a sea battle against the Corcyraeans, our own colonists, for it was not possible to find worthy opponents other than those whom we had sent out as colonists.

We proved useful to the Athenians, helping them in the war against the Aeginetans. We freed the Greeks from slavery to the Athenians, for when we were able to put a stop to their hardships we could not bear not to become champions of the wronged. We founded very many cities as colonies, benefiting Greece by the increase of our race. These were our achievements of former days. But now, in place of these good things, drunkenness, revels and costly banquets have been brought in instead. These things must be stopped by those who strive for glory.

32. 'But the plan,' he says, 'is not that of the whole city; certain courtesans of no repute, out of jealousy, privately persuade their own brothel-keepers to propose the decree against her, putting forward one man who puts on a show of decency.' You seem, man, to be eager to dignify the brothel-keepers and to want the courtesans to be held in esteem, because they practise the same craft as Lais. Hence you try to make them out to be the cause of such great benefits, not even depriving the brothel-keepers of praise. For if we granted that the whole thing was theirs, we ought to acknowledge our gratitude to them.

And I for my part would confidently say that they have made amends for their whole life, if indeed they are seen exacting from those who have offended against us a penalty worthy of their offences. But if Lais's advocates, insulting the city, call those who have been decently brought up brothel-keepers, the thing is madness, and a penalty must be exacted for the outrageousness of their words; and from this one may also surmise how excitedly they are carried away towards licentiousness.

That is why they dare to say anything at all about those who do not think as they do concerning the woman whose name I hesitate to speak often. For a wicked nature that despises the laws and has chosen to dare everything shrinks from nothing disgraceful. Hence they both plead for courtesans and refashion the names of things to suit their opinion, considering incontinence easygoingness, and temperance something savage. What wonder, then, if these men call the temperate brothel-keepers? It would belong to the same men to honour also their opposites, such as they themselves happen to be, with more dignified names.

35. Besides this, perhaps this too escapes you, that it is not possible for what is useful to come about for the city otherwise than by those who see something unprofitable [being done] coming together in common and deliberating, and, having put forward one man to propose the decree, the rest hearing it and deciding whether it was proposed rightly or against the laws.

This, then, is what was done, and the common vote ratified the proposer's motion, seeking good repute for the city. For everyone, except a few whose character you yourself lead, thinking that he was paying back the cost of his rearing to the city that nurtured him, eagerly voted for what had been well resolved; so without noticing it you are reproaching the whole city when you censure what has been decided, since you too now alone propose these fine measures, but you have, I know well, those of the same persuasion as you working with you.

37. Will you then be thought to be the only one gratifying Lais, and none of those acting with you? Certainly not. What then? If these men are persuaded by me and assent to nothing of yours, do I alone reap the good repute? Yet no one has ever said, 'The city, persuaded by this man, condemned certain people who had committed such-and-such an offence'; rather, without adding who did the persuading, everyone ascribes what was done to the city that voted, reckoning the whole to it. For as in wars, when certain men are sent out, the community of the city reaps the reputation of fortune either way, in the same way now too one must not reckon the courtesan's exile to some, so that we may not wrong many by exalting a few. But suppose, as you say, that some and not all expelled Lais: why is it any more just to bring back a woman exiled by a vote that seems right to the temperate?

38. I was very much vexed, then, when he said that the ancient lawgivers did not forbid the city to have courtesans. For the worthy guardian of the city did not notice that he was confusing what is honourable with what is not, and thinking that what has been expressly and rightly determined is the same as what has not been forbidden. For if they do not explicitly order courtesans to be prosecuted, they are not thereby commanding that they be thought worthy of honours and gifts.

'But the law does not prevent those that are here from staying.' But neither did it order those from abroad to be received. Nor has anyone written that those exiled for wrongdoing should be brought back, nor do I think it the part of temperate men. Do not, then, call your own preference law, and do not accuse the laws and the city. For it is shameful to want to win by means of the laws, yet to hold an opinion contrary to them, and to claim that the laws are laid down for good order, yet to give them over again to those who wish to live in disorder, to show them [invalid].

40. And since in pleading for Lais you mentioned the Athenians and said that many courtesans were esteemed among them, the famous Aspasia, Myrrhine, Theodote and many others, and, as if saying something marvellous, said that Phryne stands in gold at Delphi: may those who think the opposite of what our city thinks never stop admiring such women, or rather may they take Lais too in addition; but what has come over you that you hold up another constitution and laws with which we have nothing in common?

For instance, it is not the Athenians' custom to live according to the constitution of others; they have their own laws, by which they govern themselves, as they think, excellently. Why then do you force us to follow their ways? Or how are you not ashamed, collecting the reproaches found among all peoples, a slave to pleasures that not even those who have indulged in them pursue to the end? For to all, unless someone resembles this man, there comes some regret for their former errors. But of the many things you said, and all of them badly, I accepted one alone as justly said: that you used examples suited to your way of thinking when you listed for us the prostitutes from every place.

42. But if, men of Corinth, you care for good order, and we believe you care very much, this man will pay a penalty worthy of his outrageousness. And what is it? Not to attain his hope and not to see the woman he longs for; for he perhaps thinks he will seem charming to her by often reciting the decree to her on her return and recounting the contest. May the gods who guard the city not grant that this happen, exacting from this wretch a penalty befitting his impiety. For nothing is so painful to lovers as a hope for what they long for that has no fulfilment.

I think that this worthy man talks to himself in this way: 'Lais has a lovely face, she shines with bodily bloom, she gladly welcomes those who visit her, she calls those who meet her her dearest. The Graces wait upon her. To be her slave is not unpleasant. Are we then to be bereft of such a woman? Come, I will show Lais, even in her absence, that I have done her a favour, while succeeding entirely for myself.

How then will this come about? I must seem to take thought for the city, so that, finding the citizens tame, I may have them readily persuaded about her return. And I know that I shall be first of all men in her eyes, having been the occasion of such great glory for her. She values nothing above life here, for she knows the place is rich in gold. I will serve the eagerness of my beloved; I will not leave myself an excuse later to grieve my soul, that if I had proposed something about Lais I would have persuaded them. I seem already to see my dearest coming.' Having thought this (for a lover possesses a hope that consoles his passion), he did not hesitate to reveal his thinking to you.

45. The sum of what has been said is this: the choice before you now is between licentiousness and good repute. If, then, you vote to acquit, you will seem to despise temperance; but if, honouring your ancestors, you hold fast to their virtue, you will check the boldness of those who dare to say such things.

Whichever way the vote goes, it will not go unnoticed. For many sail in here; the city is a common market of Greece. Many come to us to share in the worship when we celebrate the Isthmian Games for Poseidon. How then is it reasonable for those so pious toward the gods to think worthy of such great glory a woman who readily gives up her body to those who buy it?
The ethological declamations follow.
